cards.title: Calculate true gross margin with the "all in until it's in" COGS rule
cards.summary: Define COGS as every cost incurred to get a product onto the warehouse shelf ready to sell, so gross margin reflects reality rather than guesswork.
cards.use_when: When setting product prices, deciding which sales channels to sell on, or reviewing whether a SKU is actually profitable.
steps: Apply the test: would you have incurred this cost anyway if you hadn't bought the item? If no, it belongs in COGS. Freight, duty and product purchase price fail the test (so they are COGS); warehouse rent passes it (so it is overhead).
Build the COGS stack from: supplier purchase price, inbound freight and container cost, import duty and tariffs, and anything else needed to land the product on the shelf.
Attribute lump-sum costs (a whole container, a single duty invoice covering several SKUs) down to unit level using weighted allocation so each SKU carries its true landed cost.
Compare the resulting gross margin per SKU before making channel, promotion or assortment decisions — the source argues margin is the anchor of ecommerce strategy, not an afterthought.
Recheck COGS when supplier prices, currency or tariffs move, since product-level margin can shift without any change in selling price.
caveats: The source is an accounting practitioner's guidance for statutory reporting; different KPIs such as contribution margin may be more useful internally than statutory COGS for some decisions.
Manufacturers have an additional layer of cost above simple bought-in goods; the walkthrough assumes a buy-and-resell model.

cards.title: Sort each expense into COGS or operating expense before reporting margin
cards.summary: Use a consistent above-the-line/below-the-line split so gross profit comparisons across periods and channels mean something.
cards.use_when: When preparing monthly management accounts, evaluating channel profitability (Amazon vs Shopify), or diagnosing why profit does not match sales growth.
steps: Draw the line at the point of sale: anything spent before the item sits on the shelf is COGS (above the line of gross profit); anything spent after is an operating expense (below the line).
Place in COGS: inbound freight, container costs, customs duties and tariffs, product/retail packaging, supplier discounts on purchased goods, and repackaging labour to make a return sellable.

Place below the line: outbound shipping to customers, shipping packaging, Amazon and Shopify platform and transaction fees, Amazon PPC and all advertising, coupons, warehouse rent and 3PL storage, and the cost of shipping a return back.
Keep the classification stable month to month — the value of the split comes from comparability, not from any single month's number.
Report gross margin and operating costs separately so you can see whether profitability problems come from product economics or from overhead.
caveats: Rules described are for statutory/compliance accounts in the presenter's jurisdictions; internal KPI reporting may deliberately deviate.

cards.title: Split packaging into product packaging (COGS) and shipping packaging (expense)
cards.summary: Distinguish the retail box that is part of the product from the transit box it ships in, since the two often arrive on one supplier invoice.
cards.use_when: When coding packaging supplier invoices, or when packaging spend is large enough to distort margin on fragile or gift-oriented products.
steps: Ask of each packaging item: does it sit on the shelf as part of what the customer buys? The branded retail box, inner tray and any presentation element is COGS.
Anything whose only job is to survive transit — the plain outer carton, void fill, tape, labels — is a shipping/operating expense.
When one invoice contains both types, split the line items before posting rather than coding the whole invoice to one account.
For multipacks or gift sets where the outer box is part of the offer, treat that box as product packaging and keep it in COGS.
Review the split whenever you change packaging suppliers, since mixed invoices are the common source of misclassification.
caveats: The retail-box rule comes from physical retail logic the source explicitly extends to ecommerce; there can be genuine grey areas for premium unboxing experiences — pick a defensible treatment and apply it consistently.

cards.title: Apply the drop-shipping exception to outbound freight
cards.summary: Treat supplier-charged outbound freight as COGS only in drop-shipping or free-shipping-inclusive models; otherwise it is an operating expense.
cards.use_when: When calculating margin for a drop-shipped product line, or when deciding whether to offer free shipping on a SKU.
steps: Default position: outbound shipping to the customer is an operating expense because the cost is incurred after the sale.
Drop-shipping exception: where the supplier charges the merchant a bundled outbound freight fee per order, treat that fee as part of COGS because it is inseparable from acquiring the goods.
Free-shipping exception: if shipping is not charged to the customer and is instead built into the retail price, the source allows treating that outbound cost as COGS.
If you run both drop-ship and stocked models, keep the two COGS methods separate so margin comparisons between them are not distorted.
For stocked products with paid shipping, leave outbound shipping below the line — do not blend it into unit cost.
caveats: Presented as a general rule with explicit exceptions, not a universal standard; confirm treatment with your accountant for statutory accounts.
Deciding whether to negotiate freight or find suppliers sits outside this method — that is a sourcing decision.

cards.title: Code customer returns correctly and turn returns into a second sale
cards.summary: Classify the return cost accurately, then consider voucher or exchange offers that recover the sale — noting the extra accounting complexity they create.
cards.use_when: When managing return rates in apparel or other high-return categories, and when designing return-flow offers at the returns step.
steps: Book the cost of shipping a returned item back as an overhead/operating expense, not COGS.
Book the labour and materials used to repackage or refurbish the returned item so it can be sold again as COGS — this is a pre-sale cost.

At the point of return, consider offering a voucher, discount, alternative item or upsell. The source reports success from encouraging a replacement purchase at the return step, based on the observation that the original item simply wasn't quite right.
Consider prepaid return labels at a negotiated discounted rate as a way to control return-shipping cost.
Expect the accounting to get harder when returns generate vouchers or discounts: you must track what was actually sold, at what margin, net of the incentive.
If returns are material, track return-specific metrics alongside standard gross margin rather than forcing everything into one COGS figure.
caveats: The returns-to-resale offer is reported as an observed pattern, not a benchmarked result; test it against your own margin after vouchers and discounts.
Given rising shipping costs, the source notes free shipping and free returns are increasingly hard to sustain profitably.

cards.title: Capture freight and duty against the right purchase order at the time it happens
cards.summary: Stop accumulating unattributed freight and duty invoices; attach each cost to the purchase it belongs to so landed cost can actually be calculated.
cards.use_when: When inbound logistics costs are piling up unallocated, or when setting up the purchasing workflow for a growing ecommerce operation.
steps: When raising a purchase order, record the agreed unit price and verify it against the supplier invoice that later hits the financials.
At the moment a freight or duty invoice arrives, identify which purchase order(s) it relates to and record the cost against them — do not file it to be sorted out later.
Avoid the common failure mode the source describes: a growing pile of freight and duty invoices never matched back to the products they belong to.
When one shipment carries multiple products, allocate the total freight or duty across them, weighting where the cost differs by unit (bulk, weight or value).
Treat this as a people-and-process discipline first; software helps execute it but does not replace defining who captures what and when.
caveats: Spreadsheets can work at small scale, but the source advises inventory management software as the business scales and allocations become weighted.
Specific inventory-management or accounting apps are mentioned in the source as vendor material; verify current features and integrations before selecting one.

cards.title: Move from spreadsheets to weighted landed-cost allocation as SKU count grows
cards.summary: Attribute lump-sum freight and duty down to unit level so every SKU shows a true cost, using software once manual weighting becomes unreliable.
cards.use_when: When you sell many SKUs per shipment and cannot tell whether individual products are profitable, or when preparing to scale purchasing.
steps: Recognise the problem shape: costs arrive as lump sums (one container, one duty invoice) but decisions are made per SKU.
Choose an allocation basis — the source notes you may have ordered three or four different items and the freight or duty needs to be weighted differently across them.
Do the weighting consistently for every shipment; inconsistent bases across months make margin trends meaningless.
Move to inventory management software when volume or SKU count makes spreadsheet weighting error-prone, so landed cost is computed automatically per item.
Verify that the software's output ties back to the actual freight and duty invoices you received before relying on the margins it reports.
caveats: The source flags a vendor relationship behind this recommendation; treat it as a capability requirement, not a specific product endorsement.
No specific trigger volume for switching from spreadsheets is given — judge it by error rate and time cost, not a fixed number.

cards.title: Classify supplier discounts and credits against product cost
cards.summary: Reduce COGS when a supplier discounts goods you are buying; handle credits carefully where stock has moved back.
cards.use_when: When posting supplier credit notes, rebates or discounts and deciding whether they lower unit cost or sit as income.
steps: If a supplier gives a discount on product you are buying, treat it as a reduction of COGS — it lowers the effective unit cost.
If the supplier issues a credit because stock was returned to them, record the corresponding stock movement alongside the credit note.
Do not post supplier product credits as general income; that would overstate gross margin while hiding the true product cost.
Reconcile credits to the original purchase order so unit landed cost stays accurate for the affected SKUs.
Where credits are recurring (volume rebates), decide how to apply them — retroactively to units sold or prospectively — and apply the same treatment each period.
caveats: The source hedges this point ('it depends', 'generally speaking'), particularly for credits tied to stock movement — confirm with your accountant.

input.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx
input.text:
20-FIN / finance and accounting Goes here. An interview with an accounting integrator detailing the specific rules for calculating Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) in e-commerce, including how to handle freight, duties, drop-shipping fees, customer returns, packaging, and Amazon/Shopify platform fees. Not here. • Negotiating freight or finding manufacturing suppliers -> 18-COG • Product pricing strategy and ad copy -> 03-OFF

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides explicit, practical guidance on how e-commerce brands must classify operational expenses versus Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) to accurately track gross margins and profitability. modules: [FIN] topics: [COGS, e-commerce accounting, freight classification, landed cost, gross margin, inventory management, drop shipping, customs duties] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. defining COGS / defining Cost of Goods Sold as every expense incurred to bring a product up to the point it sits on the warehouse shelf ready to sell ("all in until it's in"); freight and duty classification / clarifying that inbound freight, shipping container costs, and customs tariffs are strictly included in COGS; outbound shipping classification / noting that outbound shipping to the customer is an operating expense unless it's a drop-shipping model or explicitly baked into a "free shipping" retail price; packaging classification / distinguishing between "product packaging" (the retail box sitting on the shelf), which is COGS, and the "shipping packaging" (the brown cardboard box), which is an operating expense; platform fees / explicitly stating that Amazon PPC fees, Shopify transaction fees, advertising, and warehouse rent (3PL storage) are operating expenses, not COGS; returns accounting / explaining that the cost of shipping a return back is an overhead expense, but the cost to repackage or refurbish the item to make it sellable again can be classified as COGS; inventory management / recommending software over spreadsheets to automatically attribute and weight lump-sum freight and duty invoices down to the individual SKU level to calculate true landed cost.

Look for.

The "All in until it's in" Rule: The guiding accounting principle that any cost incurred before the product is ready to be sold on the shelf is COGS, and any cost incurred after the sale is an operating expense.

The Packaging Distinction: The specific rule that the retail box (e.g., the white Apple iPhone box) is part of COGS, but the brown cardboard shipping box it goes into for delivery is a shipping expense.

The Drop-Shipping Exception: Noting that outbound shipping is usually an expense, except in drop-shipping models where the supplier charges the merchant a bundled outbound freight fee, which is then counted as COGS.

The Repackaging Rule for Returns: Clarifying that return shipping is an overhead expense, but the labor and materials used to repackage that returned item to make it sellable again are classified as COGS.

Skip. Plugs for the A2X software tool and Outserve accounting services.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard accounting and reporting principles). Volume. ~350 words.

everyone and welcome. Today we're diving into the world of COGS. That's cost of goods sold. And we're going to talk about why it's such a crucial part of accurate accounting for e-commerce businesses. I'm joined by Phil Oakley from Outserve, one of the UK's top accounting integrators. outserve work with many well-known Amazon and Shopify brands, some you might recognize, and they help them to streamline their accounting and get their inventory management sorted out. Phil is a real expert in this space. So, if you are an e-commerce brand looking to get a handle on your numbers, you're in the right place. So, Phil, great to have you here. And tell us a little bit about yourself. >> Thank you very much. Thank you for that great introduction. No pressure there there at all. But yes, uh at outserve we have a specialist team working with scaling e-commerce businesses and and brands. And because I think we have a real focus on inventory management, inventory accounting with some of the software and the tools, we do spend a lot of time uh looking at at COGS and COGS calculations and all of those things. So really really really excited to get into a discussion uh about how we can yeah help some businesses understand. Great. So, before we get into the nuts and bolts of cost of goods sold, let's talk about why it's important to get it right in the first place. Why is close enough not good enough for e-commerce brands? Um, Phil, you tell us a bit more about that. >> I think, you know, for us, it it we talk about COGS all the time, but what we're really talking about is margin and profit. And of course hopefully that's what all the all the businesses uh are are in this in this for um especially in these you know challenging challenging times. Um, if you don't know your cogs, then you don't know your your profit margin. You you can't calculate your profit. And and I think, you know, when we think about strategy and and all businesses need to be thinking about their strategy so much at the time once you've decided what problem you're solving, you know, what great product you've got, then your cost of goods sold and your margin is really going to dictate so much of your strategy from what channels you sell on, how you promote. um it's it's really going to be the anchor of of everything in in your business uh to understand how you're going to going to make money, how you're going to be profitable, how you're going to be successful and and deliver maximum value. Um and you know, it feels to me so many times that businesses without understanding COGS are really flying blind, flying by the seat of their pants and and uh understandably giving themselves some sleepless nights maybe. >> Yes, I can imagine. So um okay so from the accounting side just tell us to start with what exactly does cost of goods sold cover and how would you go about calculating it? Yeah. And I think we could all say straight away, Ellsworth, it's complicated. It's it's complex. It's not always straightforward. And for different businesses, it it can be quite different. I think if we just try and focus at the moment on on many of the types of businesses that we would uh have as as A2X clients who are buying products in and selling products, we can touch a bit, you know, obviously if you're manufacturing, then your cost of goods sold is going to have another layer and level to it. But if we just sort of build it up and we think about business that that's buying in in in that cost of goods sold, you know, we we're we're really thinking in that calculation of of everything you've paid for that product up to the point that you've got it onto your shelf. Um, you know, think from the supplier door onto your shelf um before it's sold. And that's thinking, okay, let's always start with I've got to buy the product. there's a purchase price for that product. Hopefully, we've all know what that is. It might be, you know, sometimes even for some some of our clients that's not clear and until it's uh later on prices fluctuate and change, especially in some commodity markets, currencies change. But then, of course, the big ones we often think about is freight. It's the freight cost to bring that product in. So if you were bringing say a product in from China, which of course is is very common and popular with some e-commerce businesses, you're going to have uh probably a container maybe uh coming over by container, you're going to have that container cost, which is is going to be included in the cost of goods sold. And then of course you're going to have to think about how do you actually allocate that that complete container cost to each product. Um duties uh is is another one that we we spend a lot of time thinking about. you know a lot of discussion on on tariffs at the moment and and that affects everybody. So tariff is the percentage of the the import duty and then the actual import duty is what what you pay and of course for you know so many of the American North American uh A2X users there looks like there could be some very interesting tariffs and calculations all of that that tariff all of those import duties are going to be included in in the cost of goods sold. So, it's increasing that uh that that product product cost and and anything really to get it into your warehouse onto your shelf is going to be included in there. Um, so I think that's that's really the starting point, but also it's not just okay, what's in there then how how is it calculated? because you might have that those duties and those freight in sort of big lumps on invoices from different people and then it's all got to be attributed across essentially down to a unit by by unit cost. So you can see a total cost of of of the unit. Does that does that make sense? >> Yeah. So there's there's a few moving parts there. >> There is >> in reality we do know that a lot of e-commerce sellers struggle with this. um tell us some of the common pitfalls that you see when businesses are trying to calculate their costs. >> Yeah, and and I think you know obviously some really just do struggle to to to calculate it at all and and they're they're left with a you know sort of a zero or a QuickBooks or a Netswuite without having clear figures in their tool. So maybe they've just put all of their purchase invoices uh in there and they're not even making a making a stock adjustment. But I think some of the um you know some of the the common areas as I've sort of touched on before is that they're not actually allocating those costs to each unit or trying to understand how how those costs would would apply. I think there's a some confusion on sort of okay I've got uh inbound freight but actually I've got shipping costs out and those shipping costs in in most cases are not included. >> Yes. >> In in costs of goods sold. Maybe some people start to think that they've got to put their fees, their Amazon fees or their advertising. And it's really, you know, we start to get into this conversation, what's above the line of gross profit. Um, so what is really that gross profit margin and what's below the line and in below the line we're talking what's an overhead? you know, we might be thinking what's, you know, opex, what's an operating e expense and classifying that so you can really have some good comparison figures and and I think shipping income as in uh outbound shipping, shipping income and uh shipping expenses confuses people even you know to the point of of packaging. So, if it's a box which is actually part of of the product, so it's the product box with the picture on, that's part of your cost of goods sold as as you would expect. Um, you know, if someone over here, you can see that Apple box, that box is part of the cost of goods sold. But the brown box that it goes into when it actually leaves and gets delivered, that is not part of the cost of goods sold. That that's part of the shipping cost to go out. So suddenly you might have an invoice with with you know packing boxes on or or product boxes and they might be on the same invoice and then you've got to start splitting it down to go actually that is part of the product and that is not. And of course at every level we can get a little bit more complicated. >> You know in when we've got clients in fashion and apparel then they can have a lot of returns and many businesses can have returns and then when stuff comes back in you've got to start understanding the cost there. If if the if the cost is actually to repackage that product into that maybe to make it sellable again, that could be part of the cost of goods sold. If it's part of bringing it back and then actually then just getting it ready to to ship it out again, then that's not. So, you know, there's those that fine line between there's lots of costs going on and just really understanding which which part of of it is it is it to get it ready up to that to sell it and then it's a co cost after sale and that's what you've you've got to think sometimes is really the the shipping cost to send it out is after you've sold it. >> Yes. >> Um the brown box that it goes in is a cost after you sold it. the, you know, the product box was a cost before you sold it and and start to think about things. There's a few little rules that you can follow as in would you have incurred this cost anyway if you hadn't have bought that item. So, it's a bit like the rent of your warehouse. You would have incurred that cost whatever. Even if you didn't buy that shipment, you would have still had that cost.
